senses.gloss:
Woman, Hindu
------------------------------------------
General Introduction
If the estimate of the excellence of a civilization and culture depends upon the degree of excellence of its women, then, the women of the Vedic age and the epic period prove it beyond all doubt.
The knowledge of ब्रह्मन् of Vāgāṁ-bhṛṇī (Ṛgveda 10.125.1-8), the intellectualism of गार्गी वाचक्नवी (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.6.1), the yogic म्य्स्तिचिस्म् of सुलभा (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparva 320), the scholarship of अरुन्धती who was an ācāryā (teacher) in her own right (Mahā-bhārata, Anuśāsanaparva, 130), the wifely devotedness of सावित्री (Mahābhārata, Vanaparva 297), the consummate chastity of अनसूया (Mahābhārata, Ādiparva 65) and the perfect personification of all the great womanly virtues called सीता (Rāmāyaṇa)—these are the unique qualities of the all-time great women of India who have shown by their life and example, to what glorious heights women can rise.
Basic Hindu Attitude
This could happen only because Vedānta, the quintessence of Hindu scriptures, has declared in unequivocal terms that man and woman are two aspects of one and the same divinity (vide Śvetā-śvatara Upaniṣad 4.3; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.3). Hence, both have the same capacity to realise that divinity. Consequently, they should be given equal opportunities to do so. This is established by the examples of मैत्रेयी as a seeker of Truth (vide Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.3-5) and Vāgāmbhṛṇī as a perfected सोउल् (vide Ṛgveda 10.125).
One more basic factor has to be remembered here. Both man and woman—nay, even every living being in the universe—are, in their essential nature, the आत्मन्, the सोउल्, which is immortal and pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. For a bound सोउल् (the जीव) birth as a man or as a woman depends on its कर्म. The same जीव is sometimes born in a male body and sometimes in a female.
Since the ancient Hindu sages kept these basic facts in मिन्द् always, women were given full freedom to pursue any goal of life, here or hereafter.
Hindu Woman through the Ages
1. A Brief Survey
This is amply proved if we course through the Hindu scriptures of the early periods.
In the Ṛgveda itself about thirty women sages like Viśvavārā (5.28), Apālā (8.91) and घोषा Kākṣīvatī (10.39) have been mentioned as the seers of hymns.
Girls who underwent the उपनयन sacrament and studied the वेदस् either in the गुरुकुल (house of the गुरु) or at home were known as brahmavādinīs. The sadyovadhūs were those girls who did not study the वेदस् but were straight-away given in मर्रिअगे. But even these girls underwent the उपनयन sacrament just before मर्रिअगे.
The tradition of sending the girls to the gurukulas seems to have been gradually given up, the responsibility of educating them being taken over by the ड़थेर् or other elder men of the family.
Even during the epic period, women could undergo उपनयन ceremony, study the वेदस् and be teachers of the वेदस्. This tradition probably disappeared by the time of the Manusmṛti (200 B. C.).
By the time of the smṛtis and the धर्मशास्त्रस्, there was a gradual decline in the status of women, who were even bracketed with the शूद्रस्, shorn of all the earlier privileges. Social upheavals brought about by frequent invasions by foreign marauders might have contributed to this development.
It is a matter of great pride and satisfaction that even during these dark middle ages (from A. D. 900) many eminent women of literary fame like Ketalādevī (12th century A. D.), military generals like Nāyakādevī (of Gujarat, A. D. 1158), administrators like Ahalyābaī Hoḷkar, (A. D. 1735-1795) and saints like मीराबाई (A. D. 1547-1614) appeared on the country’s horizon keeping the ancient spirit of India alive.
With the advent of political freedom and reform movements within हिन्दुइस्म् the condition and status of women have improved a lot.
2. A Bird’s Eye View of the Social Structure
Over the centuries, the position and status of women has seen several changes.
During the Vedic and the epic ages, they had access to good एदुचतिओन् and the freedom—as adults—to choose their husbands. As wives and mothers, they had a respectable place in the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् and religious rites, though rarely, they had the freedom and opportunity to remain unmarried and devote themselves to spiritual pursuits.
However, the insecurity brought about by the frequent foreign invasions forced the Hindu society to subject women to many restrictions, practically confining them to the four walls of the home, whether parental or those of their husbands.
Pre-puberty marriages culminating ultimately in ridiculous child-marriages was one of the evil results, of this restriction. As a corollary arose the problem of child-widows who had to lead a wretched life for the rest of their lives slaving for others. Attempts to introduce remarriage of such widows by social reformers like ईश्वरचन्द्र विद्यासागर (A. D. 1820-1891) were not very successful.
As for adult widows, including those with children, healthy restrictions were imposed, in consonance with the Hindu philosophy of life. They were expected to lead an austere life similar to that of saṁnyāsins. Tonsure of widows existed only in a small section of orthodox ब्राह्मणस् in South India. Even this has disappeared now.
Remarriage of married women was permitted under certain special conditions like the death of the husband before consummation, the husband missing for a long time or taking सṁन्यास (monastic life).
Since मर्रिअगे was considered a sacrament and a life-long bond, its dissolution—or divorce—was unknown.
Though eight forms of मर्रिअगे had been mentioned by the dharmaśāstrās, only the first four—brāhma, दैव, ārṣa and प्राजापत्य (See VIVĀHA for details.)—were recognised as legal.
While the wife was expected to preserve her chastity at any cost and be devoted to her husband, the husband was required to treat her with love, consideration and respect. She too had an important role to play in religious rites.
The place of the मोथेर् in the family was supreme. By declaring her to be far superior even to the ड़थेर् (vide मनु-smṛti 2.145), she was raised to the status of a goddess. Her curse could never be averted. Even a saṁnyāsin (monk) had to bow down before his मोथेर् whereas all others, including his ड़थेर् had to pay obeisance to him!
The सती system, where the widow sacrificed her life on the funeral pyre of her dead husband was optional and was confined mostly to the princely class. It was never encouraged, though during a certain period (in the 18th century Bengal) most inhuman widow burnings did take place.
This was successfully eliminated by the efforts of enlightened leaders like राजा राम्मोहन् रोय् (A. D. 1772-1838).
Mention should also be made here of the practice of jauhar by the women of Rājaputāna. It is a type of self-immolation resorted to by them to escape capture, molestation, captivity or स्लवेर्य्, as a last resort, during war, when defeat was certain. These women dressed themselves well, took the blessings of the elders, came in a procession and fell into a huge blazing fire, sacrificing their lives. For them their honour as women was more valuable than even their own lives. This has shown to what great heights Hindu womanhood could rise in periods of national disaster. Historians have recorded at least three such jauhars at Chittor (in Rajasthan) during A. D. 1303, 1534 and 1568.
Another social practice which gradually deteriorated into a social evil was the devadāsī system. Originally, unmarried girls were dedicated to a local deity in a temple. They lived with their parents and served as the handmaids of the gods through dancing and singing on special occasions until they were married. When this ‘marriage’ to the deity became a permanent affair, it gave rise to concubinage and prostitution. Vigorous efforts by social reformers have practically eliminated this system but for some remnants in South India.
Up to the pre-independence days women did not have rights over the properties of their fathers. Their control over that of their husbands—even after their death—was very limited. However the laws by the Indian Parliament during the period A. D. 1954-1956 have brought about revolutionary changes in their favour.
A few other customs also may be mentioned here: The practice of नियोग or levirate was abandoned long back and was declared sinful in the कलियुग or Iron Age. The purdah system—women wearing veils to cover their faces—existed only in the royal and very rich families, that too in North India, probably due to the influence of Islamic culture. Even for serious crimes committed by women, the punishment or expiation was less severe. Death penalty was practically unknown. Women raped were never to be abandoned but taken back after expiations and purificatory rites.
The wife of the head of the family was the matron of the home. As regards the deśācāras—local religious customs—not specifically mentioned in the religious works, she and other elderly ladies of the family had to be consulted.
In the Modern Context
Political freedom of India has brought about political unity of the whole country. However, पर्तितिओन् has also had its tragic effects. As a result of these two simultaneous phenomena the life pattern of Hindu women has changed profoundly over the last fifty years than over several centuries.
Normally, it is the educated middle class that shapes the cultural life of a society. Hindu women of this class had been, for ages, holding on to their values and ways of life—good or not-so-good—with great tenacity. But, the sudden social upheavals due to the पर्तितिओन् as also the newfound freedom gradually unshackled them, making them venture into many new fields of life, formerly thought to be the prerogatives of men only.
Now they are able to receive good एदुचतिओन् in any field and get suitable jobs to earn their own money thereby increasing their standard of living, without depending on the men-folk of the family. This has contributed to their self-confidence and boldness in public life. It is not uncommon to see qualified and able women even in the fields of government administration, law-courts, police and armed forces, in business houses and in institutions of higher एदुचतिओन्.
These employment opportunities have had a very healthy effect on the widows with young children to take care of. They can now keep their independence and dignity.
Women now have equal rights of इन्हेरितन्चे over the properties of their fathers and husbands.
Polygamy which existed for millennia has been abolished and monogamy has been enforced. दिवोर्चे is easier and is allowed to both the sexes. Age of मर्रिअगे for girls has been raised to 18 (plus). However, women are generally marrying late, after the age of 20 or more.
Women are also exercising the option of remaining single or join the monastic organisations (for women) which was almost unheard of in the earlier days.
However, in their hurry to become ‘modern’, they seem to be falling a prey—like men—to imitate the Western culture to the detriment of the time-tested Hindu values of life. The ancient and eternal ideal of the perfect wifehood and the perfect motherhood—as demonstrated in the life of Sāradādevī (A. D. 1853-1920), the divine spouse of the परमहṁस रामकृष्ण (A. D. 1836-1886)—seems to be slowly fading. This does not augur well for the Hindu society. The earlier the Hindu women wake up to this danger, the better.
